words.title: Refactoring at AI speed, without the AI slop

article.publishedTitle: Refactoring at AI speed, without the AI slop

children: One engineer and a lot of AI agents rebuilt LangWatch in about seven weeks. The module structure, strict types and lint rules made a lot of slop impossible to write.

LangWatch is an LLM observability and testing platform. This refactor started as an experiment, and it kept proving more and more successful. We wanted to keep going and eventually get it merged, but we couldn't stop-the-world and code freeze until the massive refactor was done, we had to keep shipping. So we did the refactor on a long-lived branch and kept shipping fast on main.
Over the same 51 days the refactor branch took 9,187 commits and merged main in 30 times.

children.alt: Main and the refactor branch side by side from 23 August to 12 October, joined by 30 merges of main

children: While the branch was open, the team kept shipping. At the beginning that was business as usual, at our normal rapid pace. But as the refactor got close to done, weighing the pay-off of shipping on main against the risk of rewriting it all on the new branch got trickier.

So we built a whole harness just for this. Claude, Codex and even Kimi worked side by side, frantically porting everything new on main to the new structure, while the massive verifications kept running all day and all night.

The stages overlapped quite a bit. We spent the first two and a half weeks moving code, with few checks in place. On 11 September we read our own agents' traces and changed how we organised the work. Then came the rules, the lint and dependency work and the comparisons with main, and in the last few days a nearly three-day test drive and the upgrade trials. The release plan is still rough: cloud first, then self-hosted about two weeks later.
Eight overlapping phases: the big move, splitting the processes, isolated modules, lint to zero, matching main, decisions and migrations, the AI test drive and the upgrade trials.

children.alt: Figure 2 from Refactoring at AI speed, without the AI slop

children: Why the old app had to change

LangWatch had grown into a big monolith, with the Vite front end and its server in one package. There were so many different ways and places to put files that you never quite knew where something lived. Prisma was imported in ten different places, and any code could grab the app's shared services from anywhere. So when I changed the Slack reporting code for automations, it broke bug reporting, which is something I'd never have thought to check.

It was slow, too. The old app had 22.1 million type instantiations, and a type check usually took about a minute and twenty seconds, and up to two minutes on a bad run. I could tell when an agent was running one on my laptop, because the audio on my calls would just go to shit.

Agents make that mess worse. If you've worked in a codebase for years, you know which bits the rest of the app depends on. An agent starts every session without that, reads whatever code is nearby and copies it. LLMs also love going off on their own thing. You can give them as many ADRs as you want, and eventually they stop listening. Consistency has always made a codebase easier for people to work in, and it turns out the same goes for LLMs.

The plan was to turn every feature into a small module with its own data, its own tests and a contract (the only part other modules may use), with a machine checking the borders between modules. Then a person or an agent could change one module without reaching into the rest.

children.alt: Before, one app: 28 parts calling each other in every direction. One change spreads along the calls and reaches 23 of the 28.

children: A sketch. The swarm stands for the one old app (17,024 files). The modules are a slice of the 66; each arrow is a real declared call, and the subscribers are the real ones for trace's span received event.

It's basically microservices, just in the same process. The bet was that old-school software engineering, meaning tons of linting, could build a structure the agents aren't allowed to leave. Once the rules are strict enough, the AI gives up arguing and does what it's told, and it keeps going until the lint passes. That let one engineer directing agents do it in weeks while everyone else carried on shipping.

We wanted every module to have the same layout, clear ownership and a small public contract, so an agent that has seen one knows its way around the next, and a reviewer knows where to look before opening a file. A module has up to four packages:
Contract: the only part other modules may use. It holds the module's API interface, its input and output schemas, its error codes and its route declarations.
Process: the server side. Services, data access, event handling, transports and the module's data migrations.
Browser: the screens and drawers the module shows in the UI.
Client: typed calls that other modules' screens use to reach this one.
Every module has a contract and a process package. Modules with screens add a browser package, and fewer still need a client package.
In the API framework, malformed input gets a 400 and input that fails validation a 422, both answered before the handler runs.

children.alt: The agent module has four packages: contract, process, browser and client. Process is installed by the api, worker and tasks apps; browser and client by the ui app. All 66 modules have this shape.

children: The apps themselves (the API, the background worker, scheduled tasks and the UI) are now small entry points that pull in the modules they need from one generated list. Modules don't call each other's internals. They record what happened as events, and any module that cares subscribes.

The API framework does the same for routes. Each route is one declaration, with one line per check: which credential may call it, which permission it needs, the input schema, the audit record, a body size limit and the docs.

children.alt: A request passes credential, body limit and input checks, then the permission check. With a grant it reaches the handler and is audited; without one it is refused with 403. Types and docs are checked before any request.

children:
.post("/connect/register", …)
  .withAudit("agents.register")
  .withInput(agentConnectRegisterInputSchema)
  .withCredential("project", { keyKinds })
  .withPermission(CONNECT_PERMISSION)
  .withBodyLimit({ maxBytes, onExceeded })
  .withDocs({ summary, description })
  .handle(async ({ app, input }) => …)

That one declaration gets checked in two places. At compile time, the input and output types are inferred from the schema, and on tRPC you can't write the handler until the procedure says who may call it. Ask for a project permission on an input without a projectId and the compiler tells you so in plain English. At run time, the framework checks the caller's credential before it reads the body, then validates the input, then checks their grant on the new permissions system, and only then runs the handler.

Permissions are where an agent copying by hand is most likely to get something subtly wrong, so they live in the type system and the framework. Get one wrong and it either won't compile or gets refused before the handler runs. Before this PR, some of these checks were written out by hand in each route, and could be missed. Now a lint rule refuses any route that skips the declaration, and a route that writes without an audit record has to explain why in the code.

It took agents 11 days to empty the old app. They split it into feature packages (a temporary layout), several features at once, and by 3 September nothing was left in it. On 9 September those packages became isolated modules, so everything we wrote after that went straight into a module.
The old app went from 8,499 files on 23 August to none on 3 September; by the merge the modules held 18,823 files.

children.alt: Files in the old app fell to zero by 3 September while feature packages filled; on 9 September they became modules, which grew to 18,823 files by the merge.

children: Only about one moved file in eight came through untouched, because moving a file nearly always meant changing it too. Imports change, a dependency has to come in through a contract instead of a global, and a component loses the context it used to reach out and grab.

children.alt: Before the move 24,252 files: 9,788 kept their path, 5,579 moved, 8,885 were deleted. After: 37,718 files, 22,351 of them new.

children: So this was a rewrite as much as a move. Just over half the TypeScript lines we measured in the new code don't match any line in the old tree (we left out imports and SDKs, and a renamed line counts as new).

We had the fewest checks at this stage, so moves kept dropping UI inputs and callers, which we then had to find and put back by hand, and for a few days the branch wouldn't boot. Give agents speed and nothing to check their work against, and you get code that looks right but isn't wired up, and all the while main kept moving under us.
Merging in everything the team shipped

We had to carry every fix and feature that landed on main into a tree where a lot of files had moved or been split. Between 27 August and 9 October we merged main into the branch 30 times. Two of those were very large, with 1,282 conflicted files on 12 September and 455 on 5 October.
The 30 merges fell on 16 different days, and Git's saved resolutions replayed 2,755 earlier conflict fixes.

children.alt: 30 merges of main between 27 August and 9 October, with 1,282 conflicted files on 12 September and 455 on 5 October; each change was carried to where its code now lives and ticked off a list

children: The worst conflicts were the ones left after Git said we were done. Resolving a conflict by keeping the branch's deletion could also throw away a change main had made to that file. A clean merge could put new code back into a directory we'd retired, where nothing called it. Either way, a teammate could finish and ship a feature, and it could be missing from the working product without a single conflict marker left to find.

to make that work repeatable. It starts from the actual merge state, then asks what main changed since the common ancestor. For a file we'd moved or split, the job was to carry that change to wherever the code now lived and check the behaviour there. It also covers the cases Git considers resolved: deleted files whose changes still need porting, old directories brought back by a clean merge, and features that only landed halfway.

From 21 September we kept a written list of every change from main not yet carried across, so a missing feature became a known defect with a name against it. With the skill, the next agent could pick up the merge without starting the investigation again. Git's saved resolutions dealt with the conflicts that came back merge after merge; the agents still had to check that main's behaviour survived.
Pointing LangWatch at our own agents

After the move we wanted two things: a proper look at how the agents were working, and rules a machine could check on every change. The look came first, on 11 September, with the cost climbing fast. (We ran the work on subscriptions, so every cost in this post is what the tokens are worth at API list prices, not what we paid.)

We traced every Claude Code session on this PR into LangWatch, so at 09:07 that morning the engineer asked Langy, LangWatch's own agent, where we could save the most. Langy read the PR's traces and came back with a ranked list. By then the PR had used about $28.7k across 110 sessions, and for every token the agents wrote, they re-read 493, so we were paying above all for the same context being read again and again.

Langy's six findings: every session started 70k tokens deep; in these long sessions cost grew with the square of the turns; tool output was re-read 26 times; a polling coordinator ran for 28 hours and cost $357; the priciest model did everything; and one 14-day session was 42% of the spend.

children.alt: The rules landed at 12:53 the same day (442b11c726)

children: The rules landed at 12:53 the same day (442b11c726)

Less than four hours later we had turned the findings into rules that cut how much each agent re-reads. We shrank the instructions every agent session loads (CLAUDE.md) and moved the detail into files that only load for the code an agent touches. Agents hand over to a fresh agent after a set number of tool calls instead of piling up history, and batch their work into fewer, fuller turns. The coordinating agent stopped polling and reacts when work is reported back. We put Opus on the jobs that need judgement and Sonnet and Haiku on the mechanical ones, and swapped long sessions for short assignments, each with a written brief and its own set of files, with no more than six running at once at first.

Some of those rules helped quality too. A short assignment with a written brief is less likely to wander off into another module, and a fresh agent picking up a handover starts from the brief instead of hundreds of thousands of tokens of old history.

Our detailed logs only start on 13 September, two days after the change, and have a gap from 4 to 7 October. An agent-hour in them means active agent time, added up across agents and subagents. We first used Opus 5.5 on the evening of 22 September, which splits the log into three stretches:

children.alt: Cost per agent-hour fell from $25.10 before Opus 5.5 to $13.70 and then $10.60, while agent-hours a day rose from 51 to 73 to 116

children: Claude Code logs on the engineer's laptop, every subagent counted. Logs start 13 Sep, two days after the research; there are none for 4 to 7 Oct.

Total spend kept going up, but each dollar bought more recorded agent time. The workflow, the models and the tasks all changed at once, so I can't tell you which change saved what. The whole PR came to about $96k at list price across 555 sessions. The way we coordinated the agents grew out of that morning.

Put ten agents on a codebase at once and you get ten ways of writing the same thing. None of them remember yesterday's conversation, so anything that only lives in someone's head or a review comment gets reinvented the next morning. The rules had to become checks a machine runs, and every agent had to read the same instructions.

By the merge we had 76 custom lint rules, all errors, so there was no pile of warnings to scroll past. They cover file names and locations, imports, route permissions and a five-line limit on comments. Longer explanations belong in an architecture decision record (ADR), with a short link from the code. That keeps long, confident paragraphs out of it. Agents do love writing those.

checks what a linter can't see from one file. Its policies look across the whole tree: a module only sees another module's contract, each data-access repository belongs to exactly one module, and no module may end up calling itself through a chain of others. If an agent broke the layout, the build failed.
A rule that only says 'wrong' leaves the agent to invent the fix. Our
gives each lint message three parts: what is wrong, why it matters and what to do instead. The reason has to fit on one line. Here are examples from the rules in the repository:

: if a test makes too many calls, the error counts them and gives the limit. Its reason is that a test you can't read at a glance is where the wrong branch hides. The fix tells the agent to read calls into named constants or split the test into early returns.
: a long explanation belongs in an ADR, rather than a block of commentary in the implementation. The error tells the agent where to move it. Shortening the paragraph until it fits isn't the point.

: if one app imports another app's source, the enforcer names both roles and tells the agent to move the reusable behaviour to its owning feature or infrastructure package. It gives the agent somewhere to put the code, rather than just forbidding the import.

for adding these checks too. It asks for examples that should pass and fail before the implementation, and a fix an agent can apply without guessing. It also sends each check to the right place, so a local syntax check goes in lint, a rule about relationships across packages goes in the architecture enforcer, and taste with no concrete fix stays in the docs instead of becoming another error.

Above both sits the architecture record, one document of over 3,000 lines that says how the code is laid out and why. If the record and the code disagree, the code is wrong. The record also lists the ways of writing things we've retired, so an old pattern can't sneak back in just because an agent found an example of it somewhere.

Human decisions go in the record too, so an agent never has to ask a question that's already been answered. When an agent hits a question the record doesn't answer, it stops and asks, and the answer goes into the record as a numbered decision for later agents to reuse. Feature specs do the same job for behaviour, and if no scenario covers a change, an agent writes one first, error paths included. Skills (the written instructions an agent loads for a kind of task) grew from a handful to over 60.

Every question the agents asked came back to one person, the engineer, around 70 a day through the month from 13 September. They were questions like which module owns this data, whether something should be an event, or whether a difference from main is a bug or an improvement. The agents researched each question first, so a decision usually arrived with the options laid out, what each would cost and which parts of the code it touched.
We put the working instructions in the

. The coordinator reads the written work records and gives each lane a bounded assignment: the files it owns, the model it runs on and what done looks like. Lanes work on separate files; shared changes go back through the coordinator. When an agent hits its tool-call limit it writes a handover and stops, and a fresh agent carries on from that record. Questions go to the engineer and the answers go into the architecture record. The work itself lands in small commits.
Agent-hours peaked at about 200 a day on 30 September and on 9 and 10 October, with up to 43 agents running at once.

children.alt: The working loop: the engineer makes decisions, the coordinator briefs coding agents, code goes to the PR branch, testers walk the builds, findings go to ledgers on GitHub, and a fix list returns to the coordinator

children: In mid-September every agent ran its own checks as well as writing code. By 30 September there were 33 agents running at once, which was too much for the laptop, so from then on agents only wrote code and the heavy checks waited in one shared queue. It was also the busiest day for typed messages, with 782 of them.

children.alt: Most agents running at once each day, 13 Sep to 12 Oct; the peak was 43 on 9 Oct

children: Claude Code logs on one laptop, every subagent counted. Logs start 13 Sep; there are none for 4 to 7 Oct.
By the final days, cheap Haiku testers were finding problems and Opus was fixing them, with Codex doing research and second-opinion reviews on the side, all on the same laptop.

With the rules in place we went module by module. Once a module passed the lint and architecture checks, the same checks stopped it slipping back. On 16 September we deleted the list of lint exemptions to see how big the job really was.
Circular-dependency findings as measured: 267 on 2 October, 248 on 6 October, 159, 145 and 135 on 8 October, 73 early on 10 October, then zero, with organisation and identity kept linked on purpose.

children.alt: An iceberg drawn to scale: 7,166 lint findings above the waterline of the exemption list, 9,064 more below it, 16,230 in all.

children: We got the findings to zero one module at a time. Every design question they raised went into the record, so the next module didn't need the same conversation. A few things broke along the way:
14 September: the sign-in loop. The REST API accepted the session cookie while tRPC, the UI's other API, answered 401 to everything, so as far as the UI was concerned, no user was ever signed in.
18 September: the UI wouldn't start at all, and the test meant to catch exactly that stayed green. It turned out the test had its own exemption list. We removed it.

The circular dependencies were the most painful part of the whole PR. That's a module calling another module that, a few modules later, calls it straight back. Modules stuck in a loop like that are hard to change, test or put in order on their own. The checks flagged 26 of them among the browser packages on 8 September, but when we counted the architecture policy's findings properly across the whole tree on 2 October, there were ten times as many, and some had never been listed anywhere. On 5 October we deleted the allowed list, so every circular dependency failed the check.

The fewer links we had to cut, the fewer design calls the engineer had to make. On 6 October one knot of 40 modules was left, with billing, licensing, gateway and entitlement (the module that handles usage) all calling each other in the middle. A greedy approach wanted to cut nearly twice as many links as the layering we had designed. By 8 October the knot had shrunk, and an exact solver found the smallest set of links to remove, 32 of them.

children.alt: Forty modules start as a tangled knot with circular calls between billing, licensing, gateway and entitlement at the centre. The circular calls are removed one by one and the modules settle into layers. Organisation and identity stay linked on purpose.

children: A sketch of the knot, not the real graph. The counts are the measured circular dependency findings.

Each link we removed meant deciding who owns the data, or whether a call should be an event. The agents did the research on each one, so the engineer got the last links one at a time, with the options and what each would lead to, and we wrote every decision down.
Four kinds of fix came up again and again:
Listen for the event: react to the other module's event instead of calling it.
Move the operation: put it in the module that owns the data.
Keep a local view: push the data as an event into a view the caller builds from events.
Use config: replace the call with a config value.

The last link went at 06:28 on 10 October (licensing no longer calls gateway), and the policy findings dropped from 73 to zero. Removing one link can clear a lot of findings at once, because many circular chains run through it. One dependency stays on purpose, between organisation and identity. It's named in the rule as an accepted exception, so anyone who wants another one has to argue for it in the open.

The test drive later on meant running the whole product many times over on one laptop. You can't do that if every agent needs a Stripe account, a SAML provider and a credit card, or if forty of them are sharing one database.
A stack for every working copy

haven, our local development tool, starts a separate copy of LangWatch for each working copy of the code: UI, API, worker, databases and stand-ins for outside services. Agents can work side by side without treading on each other, or on the person at the next desk.
No secrets in sight: agents read the environment through haven, which masks the secrets in it.
Seeded on start: haven fills an empty stack with users, organisations and logins.
A feedback button on every page: leave a note, and the agent gets the selector, viewport, console and network calls with it.
A shared queue for heavy checks, so 40-odd agents don't overload the laptop.
haven itself got a lot lighter, which matters with 40-odd agents on one laptop. Idle CPU fell to about a tenth of what it was, and the shared browser needs about a third of the memory it did.

Every outside service LangWatch talks to now has a local stand-in, twelve in all. Tests can make one fail on purpose (a 429 from the LLM, a declined card, a batch of a thousand user-provisioning updates), and we control the responses, which cost nothing. That matters for quality as much as cost, because an agent can actually prove an error path works.
The twelve stand-ins: LLM providers, payments, sign-in (OIDC, SAML and SCIM), passkeys and one-time codes, GitHub, S3 storage, email, Slack and webhooks, analytics, Lambda, voice and telemetry.

children.alt: LangWatch on one laptop, joined to twelve local stand-ins for outside services

children: Agents test the UI through one shared headless Chromium (Playwright's headless shell, GPU off). It serves every agent on the machine, up to 24 at once, each in its own isolated browser session that's already signed in, so an agent never sees a password. For flow testing it reads the page's accessibility tree, which tells it straight away where the Save button is. Screenshots are kept for proof and for visual checks.

We tuned it so two dozen agents can share it on one laptop and still leave room for everything else. Images, fonts, media and animations are off, idle pages and sessions close after a few minutes, and the browser can never take more than an eighth of the machine's RAM.

It can also record any walk through the product as a script, even after it ran (it keeps each session's last 200 actions), and replay it strictly, stopping at the first step that differs. Scripts export to Playwright tests too. We aren't running it yet, but that makes a nightly replay possible. The idea is that an agent walks a flow such as onboarding once, the script replays every night with no AI involved, and an agent only gets involved when it breaks.
Checking the new product against the old

None of this is worth much if the product stops doing what it did before. So we compared the old and new versions, then ran a test drive across the whole product, with agents doing the clicking and the engineer deciding on every difference that mattered.

First we ran two comparison tools, apidiff and visualdiff, which call the API and open the screens on both versions and compare the results. They raised hundreds of findings, and for over a hundred real differences we had to decide which version was right. Our default was to keep main's behaviour and the branch's code structure. An endpoint that used to crash with a 500 and now answers with a clear 400 counts as an improvement. A field that went missing is a defect, however tidy the new code around it looks.

Then came the test drive, nearly three days of agents clicking through the whole product, from 9 to 11 October. Haiku tester agents drove the UI, Opus agents fixed what they found, and the fixes were committed as they landed. Between them the testers worked through more than a thousand flows (paths through the product, such as onboarding), and each result went in as a row on a GitHub tracking issue. Each tester claimed a row before starting, so two of them didn't end up on the same check at once.

children.alt: 1,016 ledger rows: 989 passed, 27 not recorded as passed

children: 27 rows weren't recorded as passed, and they're on the list to retest before the release. Partway through, the first tracking issue hit GitHub's limit of 2,500 comments, so we carried on in a second one. Haiku is cheap enough for this sort of work. In the last weeks it ran 37,734 turns for about $231 at list price, both as the testers and as the judge of screenshots.
Fuzzing in CI adds one more check by throwing malformed data at the product and logging anything it handles badly. Across the PR, the number of test files grew by about half.
Faster checks for the whole team

Splitting into modules also made checking the code a lot cheaper, and that helps the team building LangWatch every day, the same people who kept shipping through all of this. Before, every type check loaded the whole app as one program. Now each of the 411 TypeScript build projects is checked on its own against its neighbours' already-built types, so a change only rechecks what it touches.

A UI typecheck now takes well under a second, about 30 times faster than midway through the branch, because the compiler does over a hundred times fewer type instantiations (the work of expanding and checking types). Saving a file in development now rebuilds in milliseconds instead of a second or more. A lot of that comes from much smaller generated type files, the ones a package publishes for the packages that use it.
Generated type files: the annotation API went from 911 KB to 3.4 KB, the trace read hook from 930 KB to under 2 KB, and the agent tRPC types from 370 KB to 5 KB.

children.alt: 22.1 million type instantiations before, 174 thousand after, drawn to scale

children: There's a catch. Checking all 411 projects from cold is about six times the compiler work of the old single app, though you rarely need to. We measured these numbers at individual changes, some of them on a busy machine, so trust the instantiation counts more than the seconds.
Installs got lighter too. Installing the SDK no longer downloads a 38 MB cloudflared binary, and importing the Go SDK brings in 248 packages instead of 389, with no gRPC packages (down from 105).
Testing only what a change affects

CI follows the same borders. It used to run everything on every push. Now Nx works out which projects a change can reach, typecheck keeps every package's built types and only redoes the ones whose source changed, and only the apps a change reaches (API, worker or UI) get tested. If that step fails, all three get tested. Lint only runs on affected projects too, while integration and repository tests are never cached. The rules the agents worked under now run for everyone on the team.

We can't say yet whether CI got faster, because the first app CI runs on main after the merge all failed until a fix landed on 13 October. Before the merge, the median app CI run on main took about 13 minutes, and we'll compare once main is green.
An upgrade system for cloud and self-hosted

All of this has to reach installations that are already running, without losing their data, so we built a new upgrade system for cloud and self-hosted alike. Data migrations run in the background while the product keeps serving. Every step can be interrupted and picks up where it left off, workers hand over to the new version gracefully, and an Upgrades screen shows how far along it is.

Self-hosted installs are the hard part. They upgrade on their own machines, often without anyone from LangWatch anywhere near. Every migration rule we have (copy, never move; every step resumable; the previous release keeps working on the new schema) is there so an upgrade can finish without anyone around to rescue it.
The production image, compressed as pulled: 1,528 MB at its largest in 1.7.0, 494 MB in 3.20.1, about 253 MB after the merge.

children.alt: Figure 18 from Refactoring at AI speed, without the AI slop

children: upgradelab, our upgrade test bench, ran real upgrades from the old version on built code, under load, with crash drills. Setting up a trial's data now takes about 1,600 requests instead of over 100,000, which meant we could run trials over and over. They caught jobs lost when a worker crashed, queue floods, and stale reads on replicated ClickHouse. Working through the migration plan, we also found two outages that would have hit the very first deploy, and fixed both before anything shipped.

The trials upgraded about 2,000 organisations and 200,000 users without losing any telemetry. Fixes made along the way shrank the peak job queue at scale about fifteen times and cut the memory held by ClickHouse reads in flight to about a quarter. We measured all of this in trials, before any production release.

Cloud and self-hosted now run the same image, built from the public repository, and it's about half the size of the last release. A follow-up change after the merge (PR #8662) measured it on 13 October. The main reason is that we now build one image with only production dependencies, leaving out the development and UI-build packages. We haven't tried slimming it any further yet.

children.alt: Release images as published; the new image from the image-compat work in PR #8662, before any deliberate slimming.

children: Release images as published; the new image from the image-compat work in PR #8662, before any deliberate slimming.

We made 3,228 commits from 5 to 11 October, about a third of the whole PR in its busiest week by a distance, with 750 of them on 9 October alone. The engineer was answering questions from the test drive, from the last circular dependencies and from merging main, all at the same time.
Across the whole PR, we landed about a quarter of all the commits between midnight and 6am Amsterdam time.
Across all 51 days, 2,253 of the 9,187 commits, about a quarter, landed between midnight and 6am Amsterdam time.

children.alt: Figure 20 from Refactoring at AI speed, without the AI slop

children: Some of that was agents running investigations while everyone slept, which suits them fine. Some of it was the engineer steering them. On about 40 nights over the 51 days there were commits or typed messages between 1am and 6am (we don't recommend it).

We squash-merged PR #7536 on 12 October 2026. It carried everything the team had landed on main along the way, across almost 46,000 files, so thanks to Rogério Chaves, Sergio Cardenas, Andrew Joia and everyone else who kept shipping while the branch changed underneath them.
The refactor has now rolled out. We missed a field in the agent editing UI, and we hadn't connected NLP back up. Both reached production despite all the checks described above.

children.alt: Figure 21 from Refactoring at AI speed, without the AI slop

children: Invest in simulators early. We ended up with a simulator for everything external (LLMs, voice, S3, SQS, email, Slack, GitHub), so agents could exercise every behaviour end to end instead of just opening a page. That's the kind of check that catches a field that doesn't save.

Think hard about a strict structure and agree on it with the team before the mass editing starts, with the machine-checked rules, the decision record and the review of our own agent traces already in place. We added them after the move and spent weeks finding out what it had broken.

Be more ambitious with lints than feels reasonable. If something isn't consistent, add a rule so it has to be. That's what kept 46,000 files consistent, and it's the part I'd copy first on any codebase handed to agents.
Treat every merge from main with suspicion from day one. Changes vanished in merges that came out clean, so a clean merge doesn't prove a change arrived.
Follow a real request end to end. A green check elsewhere didn't tell us NLP was connected.
Keep inspecting your own agent usage. On a project this size, going through my own Claude Code sessions for frustrations, cache resets and rabbit holes is what made the token spend worth it. You can
Polish your own harness as you go. Every new way of checking the agents' work bought more trust in what they produced.

Be more ambitious with Jev, TypeSafe's judge model. Halfway through, we talked about using it as a linter. I tried it a little, but the context window wasn't big enough to be useful on my tests, so I dropped it. Next time I'd try it earlier and push harder, because it's one more tool for trust and against slop, next to the lints, the simulators and the trace reviews. See
how Jev compares to the alternatives

words.title: Internal Product vs Internalised Trauma: Supporting Event Sourced Systems

article.publishedTitle: Internal Product vs Internalised Trauma: Supporting Event Sourced Systems

children: Before we built anything custom we added metric reporting to the group queue, sent to Grafana. Group queue overview, throughput by pipeline, fold and map projection duration percentiles, retry distributions, dedup rates, fold cache hit rates
If you've been following along with this series (and if you have, it’s great to know this is interesting to at least you), you'll know that we recently rebuilt our entire platform on event sourcing.
covered what that gives you as a user.

covered how we built it, including several moments we're not especially proud of, but we overcame. This post is about the bit that comes after all of that: what happens when you deploy a distributed event processing system to production and need your tooling to be as good as the platform.

Every event sourcing retro, every conference talk, every Medium post with a suspiciously clean architecture diagram ends with deployment and rollout. That’s cool, but here is where it gets tricky. It will break, events will get stuck, something will cause events to get backed up, and projections will have bugs, and when these things happen, it’s going to hurt… Unless you have good observability and tooling to help you out.

So what happens if it’s 2am, you were at the pub, your phone pages you that 420 groups are blocked. You could check Grafana, SSH into a pod, yolo-ops commands into Redis until something happens, or invest in the second most important part of the system, the Internal Product. Once we had a finalised system, we invested a bit of time to make sure that issues with the event sourcing system are both observable and recoverable easily by our team, making potentially stressful or even just mundane, issues quick and easy to handle.
Grafana: the view from the window

Before we built anything custom we added metric reporting to the group queue, sent to Grafana. Group queue overview, throughput by pipeline, fold and map projection duration percentiles, retry distributions, dedup rates, fold cache hit rates (99.7% by the way, get in). The works.

children.alt: Internal Product vs Internalised Trauma: Supporting Event Sourced Systems

children: Grafana - Event Sourcing and Group Queue dashboard overview

Grafana is brilliant. Throughput charts going up means events are flowing. Blocked counter at zero means nothing is stuck. Cache hit rate near 100% means Redis is earning its keep. Two-second glance, all good, close the tab. For monitoring and alerting, it's hard to beat.

But Grafana shows you the state of the world, we can’t react or do anything super specific to our use case. When a group blocks at midnight because some customer sent a span with a negative duration, you can watch the blocked counter tick up in real time. Beautiful. Informative. But you’re powerless to make it go back down, which can be really embarrassing.
Skynet started it all, but didn’t end it all this time
The ops tooling went through two complete iterations in about two months. Here's the speedrun.

Built a standalone React app over a weekend. Named it Skynet because Claude built most of it, thanks buddy. It contained pipeline tree views, throughput charts, stat cards, queue inspector. It worked well, actually. But it was a separate application with its own build, its own auth, its own deployment. Two browser tabs. Alt-tabbing between your product and your ops tool like some kind of animal. And it was behind our VPN, so extra friction to just check overall status.
Moved everything inside the main LangWatch dashboard at
. Same authentication with additional platform team checks, same design system, same deployment pipeline. Live metrics stream to the browser, with a polling fallback if the connection drops.

children.alt: Internal Product vs Internalised Trauma: Supporting Event Sourced Systems

children: Ops Dashboard - Activity graph with pipeline, errors, and overview stats
When, not if, things go wobbly

When an event fails processing too many times in our system, its aggregate group gets blocked. This is by design. One dodgy trace from one customer blocks that one group and nothing else. Everything else keeps processing normally. The investigator (hi, that's one of us) then needs to figure out what went wrong and sort it out.
The ops console clusters them by error pattern instead. 800 groups all failing with

. Super manageable, no annoying layout shifting. From there you can unblock all of them (ClickHouse is back, just let them retry), move them to the dead letter queue (park them while you deploy a fix), or drain them permanently (for events that will genuinely never succeed, like spans from your mother in law, just throw away).
Before any bulk action there's a

option: try it on 5 random groups first (configurable up to 100), see if they actually succeed, then commit to the full batch. Clicking "unblock all 800" and watching 400 of them fail again could cause further system degradation in times where things are going haywire.

The DLQ re-drive workflow follows the same philosophy. Deploy your fix, canary 5 random dead letter jobs through the fixed code, and if they pass then hit "Replay All." Before we had canary re-drives this was an all-or-nothing affair, which can again cause further system degradation if it does not go to plan.

children.alt: Internal Product vs Internalised Trauma: Supporting Event Sourced Systems

children: Projection replay: your old data just got better
This is a true event sourcing super power, one to call home about.

In a normal system, when you fix a bug in your data processing logic, the fix only applies to new data. Everything that was processed before the fix is stuck with the broken version forever. You either live with it or write a one-off migration script and do some cowboy ops to run it on the prod cluster or waste half a day.

With event sourcing, the raw events are the source of truth. The processed views (projections) are derived, and they can always be rebuilt. Fix your fold logic, replay the historical events through the new code, and every affected trace gets retroactively updated. It’s genuinely that simple.

The replay wizard in the ops console: pick which projections to replay, pick which tenants, pick how far back, write a description for the audit trail, and smack go. Progress streams to the UI live. Cancel any time (gracefully, it finishes the current batch). Every replay gets logged with who ran it, when, what projections, how many aggregates and events.

Cost calculation been slightly wrong for two weeks because of an edge case nobody thought of? Fix the fold, replay for the affected tenants, in and out, 5 minute adventure. The events are facts. The views are just formed opinions about the facts, and opinions can always change, right?

This is my personal favourite, and funnily enough it's actually the oldest piece of ops tooling we have. It predates Skynet, predates the ops console, it's been quietly doing its thing since January 2026 while we were busy panicking about everything else.

Deja View lets you search for any aggregate in the system, whether that's a trace, an experiment run, a scenario, whatever you like, and load its complete event history. You then step through it event by event, and at each step you can compute what any projection's state would look like at that point in time. It's essentially time-travel debugging on your production data, and honestly it feels a bit like cheating.

Real example: customer messages us saying their trace is showing the wrong cost. Open Deja View, search their trace ID, click through the events one by one. Event 1, cost looks right. Event 2, still fine. Event 4: a span arrives with
and the running total resets to zero. Found it. The fold doesn't handle null costs, but now we know exactly “who what where when and why?”

The whole view state is encoded in the URL too, so you can copy the link and drop it in Slack: "look at event 7, cost goes to zero here." My team mate opens it and sees exactly what I see. To resolve it, fix the fold, deploy, replay the affected projection from the previous section, and the customer's trace is correct. Every other trace with the same bug is also correct.
Having these three tools work together is one of the best workflows we've built at LangWatch, they really do remove so much friction from supporting the platform.

children.alt: Internal Product vs Internalised Trauma: Supporting Event Sourced Systems

children: Deja View - Seeing how a projection is computed though the event stream
Part 2: Four Refactors and a Funeral
Why isn't Grafana enough to support an event-sourced system?

Grafana shows you the state of the world for monitoring and alerting, but you cannot act on it. When a group blocks at midnight you can watch the counter rise but not fix it, so LangWatch built an ops console for recovery actions.
What happens when an event keeps failing in production?

After too many retries the aggregate group is blocked by design, which isolates one bad trace without affecting others. An operator then inspects the error, fixes the cause, and unblocks the group, often in bulk with a canary step first.

Deja View is a time-travel debugging tool that loads any aggregate's full event history so you can step through events one at a time and compute what any projection's state looked like at each point, making production bugs easy to pinpoint.

words.title: Four Refactors and a Funeral: Migrating a Live System to Event Sourcing

article.publishedTitle: Four Refactors and a Funeral: Migrating a Live System to Event Sourcing

children: LangWatch is open source. Every commit hash in this post is real and clickable. You can see exactly how we got from A to B, including the detours, nightmares, all nighters, and occasional rapid dip into insanity.
, you know what our event sourcing system gives us. 300x faster, features in afternoons, retroactive data improvements. All very sexy.

This post is about what came before. Five months of building an event processing system in production, starting with something that worked at low scale and iterating it into something that handles 6,000 events/sec. Four meaningful refactors, each one a response to something production taught us that we couldn't have learned any other way (well, that's what we tell ourselves anyway). Also a commit with the message "actually use async inserts" which will haunt us professionally for years.

And of course, LangWatch is open source. Every commit hash in this post is real and clickable. You can see exactly how we got from A to B, including the detours, nightmares, all nighters, and occasional rapid dip into insanity.
One span arrives from your SDK. From that single event, the system has to:
Summarise the trace (fold all spans into one view)
Store the raw span (append to columnar storage)
Update your browser in real time (pub/sub to SSE)
Trigger evaluations (did the LLM say something batshit?)
Track SDK versions (are you on the latest? maybe that's why you have bugs)
All of that, and for every event. Events for the same trace
, different traces process in parallel. One dodgy trace from one customer absolutely cannot hold up the entire platform, entire customer, or even some side effects of that trace.

children.alt: Four Refactors and a Funeral: Migrating a Live System to Event Sourcing

children: A trace arrives, the fold summarises it, and the reactor triggers an evaluation - which is itself a new command that flows through its own pipeline. The GroupQueue sits between the event store and projections, guaranteeing per-aggregate ordering while processing different aggregates in parallel.

One span in. Trace summary, span storage, live browser update, evaluation trigger, billing, SDK tracking all fan out from a single event. Everything flows through the same global GroupQueue with per-aggregate ordering.

What actually kept us up at night wasn't the throughput or the ordering guarantees. It was keeping behaviour consistent between the old system and the new one during the migration period. Customers should have no idea anything changed under them. Silent cutover or don't bother. We don't want to take the lazy migration downtime windows from those that need them.
Initial event processing system. Checkpoints, distributed locks, full event replays.

We built an event processing system designed for the scale we had at the time. Checkpoint stores tracking the last-processed event ID per processor. Distributed SETNX locks in Redis to prevent concurrent updates. Full event replays on every projection update. Timer-based retries.
About 7,000 lines. Its own ClickHouse table (
), its own Redis cache layer, its own validation system that verified ordering before processing. Over-built for a problem we didn't fully understand yet. A monument to premature abstraction.
Worked fine at five events per second, but when we started stress testing we realised this was not only a dead end, but a mummified one.
"event sourcing 2, electric boogaloo" - yes, that's the actual commit message. We regret nothing. And no, sorry, we aren't hiring right now.
queries per span. 100-640ms each. BullMQ queue depth: climbing.
(343K rows). The maths: 50-100 spans/sec x 6-8 queries x 100-640ms each. Queue backing up. Processing latency in minutes. Not a good look for a real-time platform.

We slapped a Redis cache on the checkpoint reads. Bought us a few hours. The architecture still required 6 database round-trips per event, and caching one of those reads doesn't change the fact that the whole design was too chatty for the throughput we needed.
That Redis cache lived for one day. Not because it was bad, but because the next morning brought a better idea.
Distributed locks replaced with atomic Redis Lua queue grouping.

After a good nights sleep, with fresh eyes we noticed the next thing: distributed locks are solving the wrong problem. We don't need mutual exclusion. We need ordered delivery per aggregate with parallelism across aggregates. Very, very different things.

We decided to move to a custom group queue implementation in Redis, using Lua scripts. Redis Lua scripts that atomically stage, dispatch, and complete jobs per aggregate group. All state transitions inside a single Lua eval, and Redis even gives you atomicity for free. No lock expiry timers, and no "what if the holder dies" recovery, no consensus protocol. A beautiful win for simplicity.
-- Simplified: atomically pick the next job for a group
Thousands of groups processing in parallel. Same aggregate strictly ordered. If a group exhausts retries, it gets blocked individually. Not the entire queue, not other customers,
. Requires operator action to unblock (more on the tooling we built for this later).
Two weeks from cautious to reckless to "never discuss the 500 incident again."
~7,000 lines removed. Checkpoint system deleted entirely.

The old "event handlers" were doing three different jobs in one messy abstraction. Accumulating state, transforming events, triggering side effects. All of which are established patterns in event sourcing, so let’s adopt rather than re-invent. We split it into three primitives that each do exactly one thing.
accumulate state. Load current state, apply the new event, store the result. Left fold, state lives in ClickHouse.

The fold state itself becomes the resume point. This means we can avoid having a checkpoint table, and separate tracking. If the system crashes mid-flight, next event loads last stored fold state and carries on with no need for additional orchestration or storage. The 7,000 lines we removed were all checkpoint/lock/validation infrastructure that stopped being necessary once the fold/map split existed.

// Reactors: fire after traceSummary/spanStorage projection succeeds

The result: when you wire up a new pipeline, TypeScript guides you through it. Missing a handler? Compile error. Wrong state shape? Compile error. Wrong payload? Compile error. It's a second pair of eyes that never gets tired and never approves a dodgy PR out of politeness.

Suddenly we had merge parts being created in the 1970 partition. Our TTL policy says anything older than 30 days goes to cold storage on S3. 1970 is considerably older than 30 days. So these parts were immediately getting shipped off to S3 the moment they were written.

Then the next fold event arrives for that aggregate, tries to read the state back, and ClickHouse has to fetch it from S3. What was a 0.3ms Redis cache hit (or a 100ms local ClickHouse read) became a multi-second S3 retrieval. For every single new trace until the fold state got a real timestamp.

If you've built event-driven systems before, you've probably wrestled with the outbox pattern. Write state + "things to do next" in one transaction, poll the outbox, execute entries. Works, but polling is grim and that's another table to look after.

Reactors give the same guarantee without the polling. Projection router dispatches reactors inline after a successful fold store. Each reactor gets its own group queue job with hierarchical keys (so it can't block the fold for the same aggregate), its own dedup, its own retry.
Billing meter was dispatching BullMQ jobs from inside a map projection. Quietly committing crimes.
Replaced it with a reactor on the billing fold. Side effect fires after state is persisted. Not during. Not maybe. After.
BullMQ fully dead. Scenario execution, evaluation dispatch, all replaced by reactors.
One less piece of infrastructure. One less thing to page about. One less dashboard to check at 3am (though we built quite a good dashboard for the event sourcing system itself, more on that later).
One queue, two roles, no cups
Per-pipeline queues collapsed into single global queue. CQRS formalised.
Trace processing, evaluations, experiments, simulations: all had their own queues. Each needing separate concurrency config, monitoring, scaling. Silly.
Single global queue with typed job routing. And with that came the CQRS split:
// Worker process: consume projections and reactors

The migration: dual-write, migrate, flag, switch
The subtitle of this post says "migrating a live system." Here's how we actually did that without customers noticing.

Every incoming event writes to both the old Elasticsearch-based system AND the new event sourcing pipeline. Both systems process the same data, produce the same outputs. The old system still serves all reads. The new system writes into ClickHouse but nobody's looking at it yet.

Compare outputs. Are the trace summaries identical? Are evaluations triggering the same way? Are the billing numbers matching? This is the boring bit that takes the longest. You find edge cases. Timezone handling. Null vs undefined. Fields that the old system populated implicitly that the new system needs to handle explicitly.
Once we knew the new data was going in correctly, we migrated the old elastic search code over, converting into events, and building projections. This took days, elastic search was very very unhappy.

A read flag on each project that switches which backend the API queries from. Roll it out to internal projects first, then a few friendly customers, then gradually everyone. If something's wrong, flip the flag back. Instant rollback, no deployment needed.

Once all projects are reading from the new system and everything's been stable for a few weeks, remove the dual-write. The old code becomes dead code. Delete it.

The whole process took about six weeks from first dual-write to full cutover. The bit that took the longest wasn't the code. It was building confidence that the new system produced identical behaviour. Every discrepancy needed investigating. Some were bugs in the old system that we'd never noticed, some were bugs introduced by the dual writing process itself. I would say that process was not as smooth as we had planned…

We were using it for time-series analytics, high-throughput event ingestion, and aggregation queries. It was telling us, politely but firmly, to sod off and use something else.
Analytics dashboards need to scan millions of rows across a handful of columns. ClickHouse does this obscenely fast. The dashboards went from "please wait" to instant.

ClickHouse has built-in storage policies that let you offload data to S3 once it goes cold. Completely transparent to queries. We can set TTL per customer, so enterprise plans with longer retention just work without separate infrastructure.

Event sourcing is appending immutable facts. ClickHouse's MergeTree engine is built for this workload. It's absurdly good at appending. We need some special handling for fold projections (ReplacingMergeTree deduplicates older versions in the background), but that's straightforward.

Intermittent, the best kind of bug to investigate. The group queue has three outcomes for any job:

uses exponential backoff. First failure retries after 1 second. Then 2, 4, 8, up to a configurable maximum. Each retry re-stages the job in Redis with an incremented attempt counter and a delay score. The group stays active, other jobs for that aggregate wait behind the retry.

happens when a job exhausts all retry attempts. The group gets removed from the ready set. No more jobs dispatch for that aggregate. But crucially, only that aggregate blocks. Every other group in the system continues processing normally. One bad trace cannot take down the platform.

Blocked groups require operator intervention. You inspect the failed job (what event, what error, what state), fix the underlying issue (deploy a code fix, correct bad data, whatever), then unblock the group. Processing resumes from where it stopped. The tooling for this is... a whole separate blog post.

We also classify errors. Transient ClickHouse errors (connection timeouts, replica lag) are marked recoverable and always retry. Application errors (malformed event, schema violation) block immediately because retrying won't help.
Classify transient ClickHouse errors as recoverable to prevent group blocking.

Before this commit, a ClickHouse timeout would exhaust retries and block the group. After: it retries indefinitely with backoff until ClickHouse recovers. Small change, big difference in production resilience.

Replay: making old data retroactively better
Part 1 mentioned that we can replay your entire history through new logic. Here's how that actually works.

Say we improve the trace summary fold. Better cost calculation, smarter input extraction, whatever. In a traditional system, that improvement only applies to new data. Old traces are stuck with the old logic forever.
With event sourcing, the raw events are the source of truth. The projections are derived views that can always be rebuilt. So we built a replay system.
Projection replay CLI with pause-based drain and batch writes.

live processing. The queued events now process through the new logic too.
The result: every trace in the system gets the benefit of the improvement, not just new ones. Customers don't need to re-send anything. Their historical data just gets better.

We use this for bug fixes too. Find a fold bug that's been producing slightly wrong cost calculations for two weeks? Fix the fold, replay the affected projection, done. No "sorry, your old data is wrong forever" conversations.
Map projection replay with marker-based deferral.
Map projections got their own replay path shortly after. Same idea: pause, drain, replay, resume. Different mechanism because maps are stateless (just re-transform and re-append rather than re-fold).

We built an internal tool called Skynet (now rolled into the app as the operations dashboard) for real-time pipeline throughput, group queue inspection, failed job management, and replay controls. You cannot run one of these systems without seeing inside it. That post is about how we made it visible.
How do you migrate a live system to event sourcing without downtime?

LangWatch used a five-phase approach: dual-write to both old and new systems, verify outputs match, migrate historical data, switch reads behind a per-project feature flag for instant rollback, then turn off the old write path.
What are fold, map, and reactor projections?

Folds accumulate state by applying each event, maps are stateless one-event-in one-record-out transforms, and reactors are side effects that fire only after a fold succeeds, which avoids half-states without an outbox table.
How does the system guarantee per-aggregate ordering?

A custom group queue built on atomic Redis Lua scripts gives strict ordering within each aggregate while processing thousands of aggregates in parallel, so one bad trace blocks only its own group, not the platform.
Why move from Elasticsearch to ClickHouse?

Elasticsearch is built for full-text search, but LangWatch needed time-series analytics, high-throughput ingestion, and aggregations. ClickHouse's columnar storage, append-only MergeTree engine, and tiered TTL fit event sourcing far better.

children: At LangWatch, we process a not-insignificant number of LLM traces, agentic simulations, evaluations, and experiment runs every single week
LiveNation can't monopolise all the events

For the past couple of months we have been busy shovelling coal in the LangWatch engine room. Late last year - perhaps during a foul lapse in judgement - we decided to embark on the long and arduous journey to re-architect our platform to be event driven. Fast forward many late nights, a few sweaty migrations, and increasing the market cap of Red Bull by several percentage points, we're live and excited to share what this means for you, and how it super-charges us for 2026 and beyond 🚀.

This is not yet another lame-o "what is event sourcing" post forced into existence by marketing chasing yet another SEO trend, we hope this is actually useful. This is an update of what we’ve ended up with, why it matters for you, and some vanity metrics for good measure (couldn’t skimp on nice big numbers now could we).

number of LLM traces, agentic simulations, evaluations, and experiment runs every single week (at least 1, we promise). Every span that hits our collector, evaluation that fires, experiment result that lands, or matrix style simulation battle testing of your agent, they're all events. Immutable, append-only, timestamped facts about what happened in your AI system.
And because they're events, we can do things with them that you simply can't do in a traditional CRUD*-y* architecture.

Before this re-architecture, our platform could process 10-20 events per second. That's not a typo, but it got us to where we are today. The bottleneck was ElasticSearch - slow on inserts, which constricted how many jobs we could process concurrently. The system would eventually catch up, but "eventually" started getting longer and longer. Then you lot started scaling your AI systems and 20 events a second started to become a problem more often than not.
The new platform has been running for about a month now, and has already processed
and counting, and with that that we've seen peak throughput north of

already. Same servers, same team. We did swap out the database, moving from ElasticSearch to ClickHouse, which turned out to be an almost suspiciously good fit for event sourcing. Append-only writes, columnar storage, absurdly fast aggregations. But the real difference
, but rather the architecture on top of it.

Everything that flows through LangWatch (traces, spans, evaluations, experiment results, simulation runs, you get the picture by now) is now an immutable event, appended once and never modified. The system projects event data into whatever views it needs, on the fly, as events arrive. No polling or batch jobs running every five minutes clogging the system up with pointless checks on stale data. Events arrive, we do some clever things instantly, and your dashboards update…
type shit, as our gen-z intern would say.
We can increase event processing capacity simply by scaling out our worker count, hopefully making the majority of startup scaling pains an almost nostalgic memory.
We’re pretty sure no other LLM observability platform is built on this kind of foundation.
Feature Shipping, at an unreasonable pace
Now for some not so subtle flexing. This is the part that gets us out of bed in the morning.

When your platform is built on an event stream, adding a new feature doesn't mean cramming new fields into the data model not desired for it, writing a migration, figuring out how to backfill months/years of data, and praying nothing breaks. It means writing a small function that says "when this event happens, update this view." - yuge, and true.
Our billing usage tracking (counting every billable event per project per day across the entire platform) was an afternoon of work. Not a sprint, or a big project. An afternoon.

But the moment that really drove it home was when we replaced our entire scenario execution engine. We had a full job queue system: scheduling runs, tracking status, handling cancellation. A proper piece of infrastructure. We replaced the whole thing with event sourcing in a single pull request. Once you have an event log, you don't need a separate job queue. The events

children: Say we improve our trace processing pipeline. Better cost calculation, smarter input/output extraction, whatever (or even fix a bug, shocking). In a traditional system, that improvement only applies to new data. Everything you've already sent? Tough luck mate.

With event sourcing, we can replay your entire history through the new logic. Your old traces get the benefit of every improvement we ship, automatically. No data loss, no "oopsie, just wait for new data." The raw events are the source of truth, and the views we build from them can always be rebuilt.
We have some quick wins already live on production just as a side effect of the new system. These aren’t roadmapped or a
todo list, but ready for you now.
: your browser updates the moment a span arrives. No refresh, no polling.
: agentic simulations, via the scenario library, are now realtime. No more excuses to get a coffee here, sorry.
: real-time billing and usage calculations, per project, per day.
these should all be running noticeably faster now, which is always nice.
the entire platform should be all round snappier, almost instant loading compared to before too.
The more data you throw at the platform, the more useful it gets. More traces means better evaluation baselines and dataset sources. More experiment runs means richer comparisons.
Mo' events, mo' signal, and the system is built to handle it all.

The system is built for whatever load you need. Dev, staging, production - it handles all of it without breaking a sweat. If you've been conservative with your telemetry because you weren't sure we could keep up: we can.
And if there's a feature you've been wishing LangWatch had? Tell us. We're probably only an afternoon away from building it.

If you want to know how the sausage is made, stay tuned. We've got a proper technical deep-dive coming next, going into the guts of the event sourcing system, what we learned working with ClickHouse, and all the architectural decisions (and regrets) along the way.
We'll also be sharing how we built the internal tooling to manage all of this infrastructure. Turns out, building developer tools inside a developer tool is its own kind of sadistic adventure.

is a great starting point. For something meatier,
What throughput did event sourcing unlock for LangWatch?

The platform went from 10-20 events per second to peak throughput north of 6,000 events per second on the same servers, after moving from Elasticsearch to ClickHouse and adding an event-sourced architecture on top.
How does event sourcing make old data retroactively better?

Because raw events are the immutable source of truth, LangWatch can replay your entire history through improved processing logic, so old traces benefit from every fix and improvement without you re-sending anything.
Why is ClickHouse a good fit for event sourcing?
ClickHouse offers append-only writes, columnar storage, and very fast aggregations, which match the immutable append-only nature of an event log and make analytics dashboards load almost instantly.

What Is OpenTelemetry? Why it’s a game-changer for GenAI Apps

one open, language & vendor-agnostic standard that works the first time, no flipping it round 3 times… Plug the LangWatch endpoint into any OpenTelemetry compatible collector and watch the spans flow. To cut it short, you get more, by doing less. What’s not to love?
Observability must be a first-class citizen in GenAI
GenAI really is like people. It’s not deterministic, they don’t behave, they even answer back and

. The same prompt can cost twice as many tokens between two almost identical requests, stall and require multiple retries, or just go on an absolute acid trip and reinvent reality. Without rich traces recording prompt content, generations params, token counts, model version, latency, tool calls, and the ever growing list of features, keeping this portion in a black box is unsustainable.

LangWatch, coupled with all the benefits of the OpenTelemetry ecosystem, is essentially the Flight Data Recorder for your GenAI applications. Silently observing, tracing every prompt, token, latency spike, rag invocation, and hallucination allowing you to dive in and replay, dissect, debug, and then optimise when things (inevitably) get funky.

Our existing Python SDK used a custom interpretation of the trace and span pluming that OpenTelemetry standardises. This felt like a good option at the start, especially as OpenTelemetry at the time had no GenAI standards defined and the ecosystem was moving so quickly. But this has ended up with some less than ideal problems for us, and users alike. Hand-rolled spans, inconsistent and non-portable data structures, and a full exporter-collector we had to babysit.

Now we’re pulling up to the function with native OpenTelemetry spans, context propagation, baggage, battle-tested exporters and processors that “just work”. Not to mention incredible documentation to boot.
Plug and play, this is all you need to get started.

You also immediately have access to a wealth of LLM instrumentors, with a few of them hand-pick for your convenience on our brand new docs.
(but finish the blog first, of course).

We're committed to actively participating in Special Interest Groups and Working Groups, sharing our experience to advance the broader OpenTelemetry mission.

article.note: Featured research · coverage summary. Alex is interviewed in this article; the reporting is by The Verge. The full copyrighted article is available at the original publication.

children: The Verge interviewed Alex Forbes-Reed about developing an unofficial Snapchat client for Windows Phone. The interview examines how third-party clients could reach Snapchat’s undocumented API, the privacy risks for users, and how an official developer platform could give Snapchat more control over access.
